blocks.label: Multi-Agent Research System
blocks.narrative: A coordinator agent delegates to four specialised subagents: one runs literature and trial-registry searches, one reads full-text papers, one synthesises findings, and one drafts a cited evidence brief for a clinical review panel. Across this block the system is already in production — what follows are the failures that only surface once several agents are running together.

blocks.label: Developer Productivity with Claude
blocks.narrative: You maintain developer-productivity tooling built on the Agent SDK for a hospital patient-flow platform — bed allocation, transfer requests, discharge scheduling — much of it written years ago by staff who have since left. The agent uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and connects to internal MCP servers. Across this block the agent moves from first contact with unfamiliar code toward longer, more autonomous sessions.

blocks.label: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
blocks.narrative: Claude Code runs inside the CI/CD pipeline for a telecom service-provisioning platform — order capture, circuit activation, billing handoff. It performs automated review on pull requests, generates test cases, and posts feedback to authors. Across this block the pipeline is already live, and the questions concern making its output trustworthy enough that engineers act on it.

blocks.label: Structured Data Extraction
blocks.narrative: You maintain an extraction pipeline for agricultural commodity trade documents — inspection certificates, phytosanitary declarations, weighbridge tickets, fumigation records — arriving as scans and mixed-quality PDFs. Extracted records are validated against JSON schemas and released to customs brokerage and settlement systems. Across this block the pipeline is under pressure to handle more volume with the same review team.

questions.stem: A brief on non-pharmacological management of chronic pain comes back covering physiotherapy in depth and nothing else. The panel expected psychological, procedural and device-based approaches as well. The run logs show four subagents dispatched, fourteen searches executed, and every result accurate and well-sourced for the query it was given. Where does the failure sit?
options: The search subagent's queries were too narrow in their keyword coverage for the request.
The synthesis subagent failed to detect that entire categories of evidence were missing.
The coordinator partitioned the research space too narrowly before it delegated anything.
The full-text subagent screened out non-physiotherapy papers during its relevance filtering.

whyRight.text: Task decomposition is the coordinator's most critical responsibility. When every subagent executes correctly but the output misses whole areas, the fault is upstream of all of them: the coordinator assigned the wrong ground. The corpus's canonical form of this is a request about creative industries decomposed into visual-art subtasks only.

whyWrong.text: The stem rules this out — each subagent returned accurate results for the queries it was given. Query quality inside an assignment is a different failure from an assignment that never covered the ground.
Gap detection is real and belongs to the coordinator's refinement loop, not the synthesis subagent. Even a perfect gap flag cannot recover evidence that was never searched for.
Screening operates within the scope handed down to it. A filter that correctly rejects out-of-scope papers is behaving properly when the scope itself was drawn too tightly.

questions.stem: The coordinator's prompt reads: "Step 1, search the trial registry. Step 2, open the first eight results. Step 3, summarise each in 120 words." The briefs come back uniformly shallow, and when a registry search surfaces nothing useful the run still produces eight summaries of marginal trials rather than widening its search. What should change?
options: Replace the numbered steps with the brief's goal and explicit quality criteria, letting the coordinator decide how to decompose.
Add a fourth step instructing the coordinator to discard marginal trials before summarising them.
Increase the number of search subagents so more registries are covered on every run.
Move the numbered steps into each subagent's system prompt rather than the coordinator's.

whyRight.text: Coordinator prompts should state research goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedure. A procedural script locks the system into behaviour that breaks the moment reality deviates from it — which is exactly what producing eight summaries of marginal trials demonstrates. Goal-oriented prompts let the coordinator adapt as findings emerge.

whyWrong.text: Adding a step deepens the rigidity that caused the problem. Each new step is another instruction that assumes the previous step's results took a predictable shape.
More agents executing a bad script produce more output from the same flawed procedure. The script is the defect, not the throughput.
Relocating a procedural script does not make it adaptive; it distributes the same rigidity one level down and removes the coordinator's ability to adjust the plan at all.

questions.stem: Two tools are available to the search subagent: `search_trial_registry` ("Finds studies") and `search_publication_index` ("Finds published research"). Both accept a free-text query string and both return title-and-abstract records. Logs from the past fortnight show registry lookups being routed to the publication index on roughly 40% of calls. What is the first thing to fix?
options: Add a routing layer that inspects each query and pre-selects the tool before the call is made.
Merge both into a single `search_evidence` tool that queries both back-ends internally.
Add few-shot examples to the subagent prompt showing eight correctly routed queries.
Expand both descriptions with accepted inputs, example queries, and when each is preferred over the other.

whyRight.text: Tool descriptions are the primary input Claude uses to select a tool. Two near-identical one-line descriptions over similar input types give the model nothing to discriminate on. When misrouting occurs, check descriptions first — before adding classifiers or examples.

whyWrong.text: A pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure that bypasses the model's own language understanding while leaving the underspecified descriptions in place. It treats the symptom.
Consolidating into one tool loses the semantic precision that lets the model target the right back-end, and pushes the same routing decision inside the tool where the model cannot reason about it.
Examples add token overhead without fixing the root cause. They can help at the margins for genuinely ambiguous cases, but here the descriptions themselves carry no distinguishing information.

questions.stem: A panel request covers three independent questions: current first-line therapy, adverse-event rates, and cost-effectiveness. The coordinator issues one `Task` call, waits for it to return, then issues the next, and a full brief now takes about eleven minutes. All three questions need the same baseline patient-population context. Which approach uses the architecture correctly?
options: Chain the three calls so each subagent receives the preceding subagent's findings as its input.
Emit all three `Task` calls in a single coordinator response, each carrying the shared population context.
Merge the three questions into one `Task` call so a single subagent sees the whole request at once.
Spawn the three calls across three separate coordinator turns to keep each subagent's context small.

whyRight.text: Multiple `Task` calls emitted in a single coordinator response execute in parallel. The three questions are independent, so there is nothing to gain from serialising them — and the shared population context is passed explicitly into each subagent prompt, since subagents inherit nothing automatically.

whyWrong.text: Chaining creates a dependency that does not exist. Adverse-event rates do not depend on the cost-effectiveness finding, so sequencing them only adds latency and lets one slow branch block the others.

Collapsing three distinct questions into one subagent forfeits the separation of responsibilities that makes each investigation focused, and reintroduces the attention dilution that decomposition exists to avoid.
Issuing `Task` calls across separate turns is precisely what makes them run sequentially. Parallelism requires them in one response — this option keeps the current behaviour and merely renames it.

questions.stem: The brief's conflict section reports: "One source states prevalence at 8%, another at 13% — contradiction." On inspection the two figures come from national surveys five years apart, and both are correct for their own period. Three such false conflicts appeared last month, and the panel has begun distrusting every conflict the system flags. What is the underlying problem?
options: Subagent outputs carry no publication or collection date, so ordinary temporal change reads as disagreement.
The synthesis subagent should reconcile numeric differences internally instead of surfacing them to the panel.
Conflict detection belongs in the report subagent, which is the only component holding the full brief.
The two sources should have been ranked by credibility so the stronger figure could be reported alone.

whyRight.text: Without publication or data-collection dates in the structured output, temporal differences get misinterpreted as contradictions. The corpus's example is exactly this shape: a 2023 source saying 10% and a 2024 source saying 15% describe growth, not disagreement.

whyWrong.text: Silently reconciling conflicts is the opposite of the required behaviour. Genuine conflicts must be preserved with attribution and passed up for a human or the coordinator to reconcile.
Relocating the check does not supply the missing dates. Whichever component compares the two figures will draw the same false conclusion from undated inputs.
Both sources are credible and both are accurate for their period; discarding one destroys real information. Ranking is not the mechanism for resolving an apparent conflict that dates would dissolve.

questions.stem: The full-text subagent times out on a publisher endpoint after retrying twice, having already parsed nine of the fourteen papers assigned to it. It returns `{"status": "failed"}` to the coordinator, which logs that string and abandons the entire run, discarding the nine parsed papers with it. Which two changes follow the structured error-propagation pattern? Select two.
options: Return the failure type, the endpoint attempted, the nine parsed papers, and a suggested alternative source.
Have the coordinator treat any subagent failure as fatal, so no partial brief can reach the panel.
Let the subagent resolve transient timeouts locally and escalate only what it cannot resolve itself.
Have the subagent report success with an empty result set so the run continues without interruption.
Move all error handling into the report subagent, which assembles the final output for the panel.

whyRight.text: A failing subagent must return structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — so the coordinator can decide between retry, reroute, partial continuation and escalation. Transient failures should be handled at the subagent level first; only unresolvable errors propagate upward, and never as a bare status.

whyWrong.text: Terminating the whole workflow for one subagent failure is explicitly forbidden. Nine parsed papers are real progress, and graceful degradation with coverage annotation is the sanctioned response.
Reporting success while masking a failure is the worst available option: it converts an access failure into a false finding that no downstream component can detect.
The report subagent sits at the end of the pipeline and has neither the failure context nor the authority to retry or reroute. Recovery decisions belong to the coordinator.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent returns a draft covering adult populations thoroughly and saying nothing about the paediatric subgroup the request named. Reviewing the run shows the searches that executed never targeted that subgroup, and the registry does hold paediatric trials for this indication. The coordinator now holds the draft. What should the architecture do at this point?
options: Ship the draft with a note that paediatric evidence requires further research before the panel meets.
Grant the synthesis subagent search access so it can fill gaps it identifies in its own draft.
Have the coordinator evaluate the draft, re-delegate targeted paediatric queries, then re-invoke synthesis.
Re-run the pipeline from the beginning with the paediatric subgroup added to the original brief.

whyRight.text: The coordinator owns gap evaluation and loop termination. On finding a gap it re-delegates targeted queries to the search and analysis subagents, then re-invokes synthesis with the enriched findings, repeating until coverage is sufficient. Synthesis is not necessarily one-shot.

whyWrong.text: Coverage annotation is for gaps that cannot be recovered — sources genuinely unreachable. It is not a substitute for the refinement loop when re-delegation is available and the subgroup was simply never searched.

Giving synthesis its own search capability breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling. A synthesis agent with search access starts conducting open-ended research instead of synthesising.
A full re-run discards the adult evidence already gathered correctly and pays for it again. Targeted re-delegation adds only the missing ground.

questions.stem: The search subagent has accumulated nineteen tools as new evidence sources were integrated over two years. It now selects the wrong source tool on roughly one call in four. The document subagent, holding five tools, almost never misroutes. Both run the same model on similarly structured prompts. What should change first?
options: Rewrite all nineteen descriptions with sharper boundaries and a worked example for each tool.
Cut the search subagent's tool set to the four or five sources its role actually requires.
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so the subagent is forced to commit to a tool call.
Split the nineteen tools across two search subagents that the coordinator invokes in turn.

whyRight.text: Tool count itself degrades selection reliability by expanding the decision space the model must discriminate across on every turn. The corpus uses these very numbers — 18 tools versus 4–5 — and the contrast with the five-tool document subagent isolates count as the variable. Reduce the decision space first.

whyWrong.text: Better descriptions help, but they do not remove the underlying problem: nineteen candidates on every turn means more overlap and more near-miss descriptions no matter how carefully each is written.
`{"type": "any"}` guarantees that some tool is called; it does nothing to make the right one more likely. The failure here is selection among tools, not failure to call one.
Splitting nineteen tools in half still leaves roughly ten per agent — above the reliable band — and the split is arbitrary rather than aligned to a role, which is what scoping is supposed to follow.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent's draft ignores three high-quality trials the search subagent surfaced earlier in the same run. The coordinator's own conversation history contains all three, complete with abstracts and effect sizes. The synthesis subagent's prompt instructs it to "synthesise all findings gathered so far" and says nothing further. What explains the omission?
options: The synthesis subagent's context window filled before it reached the trial records in its input.
The phrase "all findings gathered so far" is too abstract for the model to act on reliably.
The search subagent returned the three trials after synthesis had already been invoked.
Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history, so the trials were never in the synthesis prompt.

whyRight.text: Subagents have isolated context: they see only what the coordinator explicitly includes in their prompt, not the coordinator's conversation history. An instruction to synthesise "all findings" cannot reach data the subagent never received. The coordinator must pass prior subagent results into the synthesis prompt.

whyWrong.text: A full context window would truncate or degrade across the input generally, not omit exactly the three records that live outside the prompt. Nothing in the stem indicates a size problem.
Instruction vagueness is a real failure mode, but no rewording helps here — the referenced findings are absent from the subagent's context entirely.
The stem places the search results earlier in the same run. A timing race would be a different defect, and it would not be fixed by anything in the synthesis prompt.

questions.stem: Combined subagent output reaching the synthesis step runs to roughly 80,000 tokens per brief. Sampling of recent drafts shows they reliably reflect the opening sections and the closing conclusions, while findings positioned in the middle of that input are omitted or garbled. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Rotate which subagent's output is placed first on each run so no agent sits in the middle every time.
Compress the combined input below 20,000 tokens before it reaches the synthesis step.
Lead with a key-findings summary and add explicit section headings throughout the input.
Insert an intermediate summarisation agent between the subagents and the synthesis step.

whyRight.text: This is the lost-in-the-middle pattern: reliable processing at the beginning and end of long input, degraded attention in the middle. The mitigation is to put critical information in the most reliably processed position and add section headings that help the model navigate mid-input content.

whyWrong.text: Rotation moves which findings get lost without changing how many do. The attention pattern is a property of position in long input, not of which agent produced the text.
Aggressive compression to a quarter of the size risks discarding critical information outright — trading a retrieval problem for a data-loss problem.

An intermediate agent adds latency and another point of failure. Where the volume itself is the issue, the sanctioned fix is having upstream agents emit structured key facts rather than verbose content.

questions.stem: While drafting, the synthesis subagent needs to confirm single facts — a dosage figure, a sample size — dozens of times per brief. Routing each check through the coordinator adds a full round-trip and is now the slowest part of the run, so the team proposes giving it broad search access. Which three statements are correct? Select three.
options: A narrowly scoped `verify_fact` tool serves the high-frequency need without granting open research capability.
Broad search access invites the synthesis subagent to conduct open-ended research instead of synthesising.
Complex research questions should still route back through the coordinator to the research subagents.
Per-subagent tool restrictions exist mainly to reduce the token cost of the tool definitions.
Every subagent should hold the full catalogue so any agent can recover from another agent's failure.
Routing all fact checks through the coordinator is correct regardless of how frequent they are.

whyRight.text: Strict role scoping has one sanctioned exception: a high-frequency need that would otherwise force constant coordinator round-trips justifies a narrowly scoped cross-role tool, while complex cases still route through the coordinator. Broad access produces exactly the cross-specialisation misuse the scoping exists to prevent.

whyWrong.text: Tool restrictions are the mechanism for separation of responsibilities and least privilege. Token cost of definitions is incidental; the reason is behavioural containment.
Giving every agent the full catalogue "for flexibility" is named as an anti-pattern — agents with tools outside their specialisation tend to misuse them.
Correct scoping, wrong conclusion. The round-trip overhead on a high-frequency need is exactly the situation scoped cross-role tools exist to relieve.

questions.stem: A registry query for trials in a rare indication legitimately returns no matches, which is itself a useful finding for the brief. The tool reports that outcome as `isError: true`. The coordinator responds by retrying the identical query twice and then escalating the whole run as blocked. What is the correct signal for this outcome?
options: Success with an empty result set, so the coordinator can record "no trials found" as a genuine finding.
`isError: true` with `isRetryable: false`, so the coordinator stops retrying immediately.
`isError: true` with a business-rule category, since no data was returned to the caller.
Success with a warning field set, so the coordinator can judge whether the absence matters.

whyRight.text: An empty result is a successful query with no matches — not an error. Signalling it as success with an empty result set lets the agent confidently report "no trials found". Conflating the two makes the agent retry or escalate a query that worked perfectly.

whyWrong.text: This stops the retry loop but keeps the false premise that something failed. The coordinator still cannot distinguish "the registry has no such trials" from "the registry could not be reached".
Business-rule errors describe an action the policy disallows, such as a refund outside its window. A query returning zero rows violates no rule — it answers the question.
The result is unremarkable, not anomalous. Dressing a valid empty answer as a warning invites the same over-reaction in a quieter form.

questions.stem: Of the five evidence categories the brief requires, two came back empty because their sources were unreachable for the whole run and the retry budget is exhausted. The synthesis subagent holds usable material for the other three categories, and the review panel sits in an hour. What should it produce?
options: An error to the coordinator, on the grounds that two required inputs are missing.
A complete synthesis over the three available categories, annotated to mark where evidence is absent.
A synthesis over the three categories, presented without reference to the two that are missing.
A held draft, pending the coordinator retrying the unreachable sources until they respond.

whyRight.text: Graceful degradation: complete the synthesis on available data, annotate coverage to mark which conclusions are well-supported and where gaps exist, and propagate that uncertainty upward. The panel gets usable analysis and an honest account of its limits.

whyWrong.text: Returning an error because input is incomplete discards three categories of correctly gathered evidence and leaves the panel with nothing.
Proceeding without noting the gaps is the more dangerous failure: the panel reads a partial brief as a complete one, with no signal that two categories were never covered.
The sources were unreachable for the entire run, so this is an unrecoverable gap rather than a transient one — and blocking indefinitely against a fixed deadline guarantees no output at all.

questions.stem: A six-hour brief run crashes with the search and document subagents complete and synthesis half-finished. Restarting re-executes everything from the beginning, including the ninety searches that already succeeded, and the team has now lost two afternoons this way. Which two changes let the coordinator resume from where it stopped? Select two.
options: Each subagent exports its status, findings, coverage and gaps to a known location as it works.
The coordinator reads a manifest of subagent states on restart and injects completed findings into prompts.
Each subagent holds its findings in its own context window until the coordinator asks for them.
The coordinator relies on the conversation history surviving the crash and continues from that point.
The run is split into six one-hour runs so that any single crash destroys proportionally less work.

whyRight.text: Structured state persistence: each agent exports its state to a known location, and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume, injecting persisted findings into agent prompts and continuing from the checkpoint rather than re-running the full investigation.

whyWrong.text: Findings held only in a subagent's context window fill that window and survive nothing. A crash destroys them exactly as it destroys everything else in memory.
The API is stateless and an interrupted session's context is gone. There is no conversation history to rely on after the process dies.
Chopping the run into smaller pieces reduces the blast radius without creating any resume capability — each piece still restarts from zero, and the work is not checkpointed.

questions.stem: Your evidence sources are exposed to the agent as an MCP resource listing every available registry, its coverage window and its field schema. A teammate reviewing the design argues this should have been a `list_sources` tool instead, since the agent could then request only the registries it needs. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
options: A tool is read on demand as context, whereas a resource has to be invoked by the model.
Resources and tools are interchangeable here; the choice affects only how the server is documented.
A resource can accept parameters and filter its output, which a tool is unable to do.
A resource is read as context without the model choosing to call it; a tool requires the model to invoke it.

whyRight.text: Resources expose content catalogs the agent reads as context, giving it an immediate map of what data exists. A tool adds an LLM call and depends on the agent remembering to invoke it first — which is the failure mode a catalog is meant to remove.

whyWrong.text: This states the distinction backwards. Tools are the primitive the model invokes; resources are read-only data made available to it.
The two primitives behave differently at runtime: one is available as context, the other costs a model decision and a call. That difference is the whole reason to prefer a resource for a catalog.
Parameterised, filtered access describes a tool, not a resource. Resources are read-only data exposed for the agent to consult.

questions.stem: You ask the agent to add test coverage to the discharge-scheduling module, which currently has none and which nobody remaining fully understands. Two decomposition strategies are on the table: a predetermined sequence of steps fixed before any code is read, or subtasks generated from what each step uncovers. Which is appropriate here?
options: The predetermined sequence, because a fixed pipeline produces reproducible results across runs.
Dynamic adaptive decomposition — map the structure, prioritise by risk, and adapt as dependencies surface.
A single comprehensive prompt covering discovery, prioritisation and test authoring together.
The predetermined sequence, with a manual review gate inserted after each of its steps.

whyRight.text: The scope is unknown up front, so each step depends on what the previous one revealed — the defining condition for dynamic adaptive decomposition. The corpus walks this exact task: map structure with Glob and Grep, find the untested modules, prioritise by risk, then adapt when an external dependency appears and needs a mock.

whyWrong.text: Fixed pipelines suit predictable structures where all steps are known in advance. Here the dependencies are unknown, so a script written before discovery cannot react to what discovery finds.
One giant prompt covering everything produces attention dilution — deep on some areas, shallow on others. Decomposition exists to prevent this.
Review gates control when a human intervenes; they do not give the plan the ability to change shape when an unanticipated dependency appears mid-task.

questions.stem: A deprecated `assignBedByPriority` helper is being removed, and you need every location that calls it across a repository whose naming conventions drifted years ago. An engineer proposes running Glob over `**/assignBedByPriority*` and reports that it returned two files, both of them tests. What is wrong with that, and what should run instead?
options: Nothing is wrong — Glob is the right tool and that pattern will match every calling file.
Glob is right but the pattern is too narrow; widening it to `**/*assignBed*` catches the renamed files.
Glob is too slow across a repository this size; Bash with `grep -r` is the practical alternative.
Glob matches file paths rather than file contents — Grep for the identifier finds the call sites.

whyRight.text: Glob is file-path pattern matching; Grep is content search. Call sites are file *content*, so Glob over the function name finds only files whose *names* contain it — almost certainly none of the callers. The corpus uses this exact contrast for locating references to a deprecated function.

whyWrong.text: The pattern matches paths, not code. A file called `orderService.ts` that calls the helper on line 40 is invisible to any path glob.
Widening a path pattern widens the set of *filenames* considered. No path pattern can reach inside a file to find an identifier.
Performance is not the defect, and reaching for Bash bypasses the tool designed for content search. Grep is the built-in for this job.

questions.stem: The agent applies your transfer-request audit-logging convention in some sessions and ignores it in others, on the same repository and the same files. The instruction is definitely written down somewhere, and a colleague working on the same codebase sees it applied every single time. What is the first diagnostic step?
options: Run `/memory` to list which memory files are actually loaded in each session.
Restate the convention at the top of every prompt so that it cannot be missed.
Move the convention into `.claude/rules/` with a glob covering the transfer-request files.
Copy the convention into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so that it loads for every project you open.

whyRight.text: `/memory` shows which memory files are loaded in the current session, and it is the first diagnostic whenever Claude follows a rule sometimes but not always. Before changing where the instruction lives, establish whether the file holding it is actually being discovered.

whyWrong.text: Repeating the instruction louder each session treats the symptom. It also abandons the configuration mechanism that is supposed to make the convention automatic.
Path-scoped rules may well be the right destination, but choosing a destination before diagnosing which files load is a guess. Confirm what is loaded first.
User-level config is not shared through version control, so this fixes your machine and leaves every teammate with the original inconsistency.

questions.stem: Yesterday's named session mapped the bed-allocation call graph in depth, and that analysis is still largely valid. Overnight another team refactored three of the roughly forty files it examined. You need to continue the same investigation today without paying for the whole mapping again. What is the right way to resume?
options: Start a fresh session and re-analyse the whole call graph so nothing rests on stale results.
Resume the named session and carry on, since the great majority of the analysis is unaffected.
Resume the named session and tell it exactly which three files changed, for targeted re-analysis.
Start a fresh session and inject a summary of yesterday's conclusions rather than resuming.

whyRight.text: When you resume after code has changed, name the changed files so the agent re-analyses just those rather than trusting stale tool results or re-exploring everything. Most of the prior context is still valid, which is what makes resumption the right base.

whyWrong.text: Re-analysing the entire call graph discards a large body of still-valid work. Full restarts are for when context has genuinely degraded, not when three files moved.
Resuming without flagging the changes leaves the agent reasoning over stale tool results for exactly the files that changed — the specific failure this rule exists to prevent.
Fresh-plus-summary is the correct choice when prior tool results are broadly stale. Here they are broadly current, so it throws away usable detail for no gain.

questions.stem: The agent attempts to Edit a status constant in a 900-line scheduling file. The anchor text it selected appears in four places, and the edit fails with a non-unique-match error. The agent proposes retrying with a shorter anchor that it expects will be easier to locate. What should happen instead?
options: Retry with a shorter, more generic anchor so that a match is easier to locate.
Read the file, modify the content programmatically, and Write the updated version back.
Use Bash with `sed` to force the replacement across all four occurrences at once.
Split the file into smaller modules first, so that each anchor becomes unique.

whyRight.text: Edit works by unique text matching, and its sanctioned fallback when no unique anchor exists is Read, modify, Write — a reliable full-file modification.

whyWrong.text: A shorter anchor is *more* likely to be non-unique, not less. This makes the failure more certain while appearing to address it.
Forcing the replacement through `sed` bypasses the tools designed for the job and changes all four occurrences when only one was targeted.
Restructuring a 900-line file to work around a failed edit is a large, risky change in service of a small one, and the constant may still repeat after the split.

questions.stem: The agent generates a bed-reassignment routine, reasons at length about edge cases in its own output, and concludes the approach is correct. Asked in the same conversation to check its work again, it confirms the result. Two subtle defects surface in human review a week later. Which two changes address the cause? Select two.
options: Send the finished routine to a separate instance that never sees the generation reasoning.
Give that reviewing instance only the artefact and the review criteria, not the conversation.
Add "review your own work thoroughly before finishing" to the generation prompt.
Enable extended thinking on the generating instance so it considers more edge cases.
Ask the same conversation for a second review pass once the routine is complete.

whyRight.text: A model that generated code retains its generation reasoning and is anchored to its own decisions. True independence means a separate instance receiving only the artefact and the criteria — without the justifications the generator already talked itself into.

whyWrong.text: Self-review inside the same context inherits the same anchoring. The instance re-reads its own reasoning and confirms it.
More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny. Extended thinking deepens the existing line of thought rather than challenging it.
A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context. Same-conversation second pass does not equal independent review.

questions.stem: A `/trace-dependencies` skill walks the scheduling module's imports and returns several thousand lines of output into the conversation. After it runs, the agent has lost track of the refactor it was carrying out beforehand and begins proposing unrelated changes. Which frontmatter change fixes this?
options: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent context.
`allowed-tools: [Read, Grep]`, so the skill cannot write anything while it walks.
`argument-hint`, so the skill can be scoped to one package per invocation.
`description`, rewritten so the skill triggers only when dependency tracing is requested.

whyRight.text: `context: fork` runs a skill in an isolated subagent context so its output does not pollute the main conversation window. This is the corpus's named use case for exactly this symptom — a large-output skill causing the agent to lose the original task.

whyWrong.text: Scoping tools controls what the skill may do, not how much output it returns into the main context. A read-only skill can still flood the window.
Narrowing the scope shrinks each run's output but leaves the pollution mechanism intact, and the task still needs the full dependency picture.
The description governs when the skill is offered, not what happens to its output once it runs. The context loss occurs on the runs you intended.

questions.stem: A colleague's in-house harness wraps the API and keeps calling until the response text no longer contains the word "next". It sometimes halts mid-task with tool calls still unexecuted, and sometimes keeps looping long after the work is finished. What should drive the loop instead?
options: A maximum iteration count, so that a runaway loop always terminates within a fixed budget.
The presence of unexecuted tool calls in the harness's own pending queue.
A timeout measured from the first request, after which the harness returns what it has.
The `stop_reason` on each response — continue on `tool_use`, stop on `end_turn`.

whyRight.text: The orchestrator inspects `stop_reason` after each call to decide whether to continue: `tool_use` means execute the tool, append the result and call again; `end_turn` means Claude has finished. Loop control is driven by that field, not by text content or iteration count.

whyWrong.text: An iteration cap is a safety backstop, not a termination condition. It cannot tell a finished task from an unfinished one — it stops both at the same number.
The queue reflects what the harness has already parsed out of a response. The authoritative signal about whether Claude intends to continue is `stop_reason` on the response itself.
A wall-clock timeout truncates slow work and lets fast runaway loops continue unchecked. It is orthogonal to whether the model has finished.

questions.stem: Two tasks are queued: replacing the scheduling engine's persistence layer across roughly fifty files, where several designs are viable and the choice affects every caller, and fixing a null-dereference crash with a clear stack trace in a single file. Which pairing of modes is correct?
options: Direct execution for both; switch the persistence work to planning mode if it turns out to be difficult.
Planning mode for both, since any change to a clinical system warrants a reviewed plan first.
Planning mode for the persistence replacement; direct execution for the null-dereference fix.
Direct execution for the persistence replacement; planning mode for the crash, which needs diagnosis.

whyRight.text: Planning mode suits large scope, architectural decisions and multiple viable approaches — a fifty-file persistence replacement is the corpus's own example class. A single-file fix with a clear stack trace has defined scope and a known approach, so direct execution applies.

whyWrong.text: Starting in direct execution and switching when it gets hard is named as a trap. Reactive switching is expensive because the premature work has to be unwound.
Domain sensitivity is not the selection criterion. Planning mode is chosen on scope and design ambiguity; a clear single-file fix gains nothing from a plan.
This inverts both. A stack trace has already done the diagnosis, and the fifty-file change is precisely where premature execution costs the most rework.

questions.stem: An expensive analysis of the transfer-request state machine has just completed, having taken most of an afternoon. The team wants to evaluate two migration strategies against that analysis, and wants neither evaluation coloured by the other's reasoning or conclusions. What should they do?
options: Use `fork_session` twice from the completed analysis, evaluating one strategy in each branch.
Evaluate both strategies sequentially in the current session, then compare the two write-ups.
Start two fresh sessions, each re-running the state-machine analysis before evaluating its strategy.
Evaluate the first strategy, then use `--resume` on the same session to evaluate the second.

whyRight.text: `fork_session` creates branches that inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently. That is exactly the requirement: one expensive shared baseline, two evaluations that cannot contaminate each other.

whyWrong.text: The second evaluation is biased by the first's reasoning and conclusions, which sit in the same context. That is the contamination the team explicitly wants to avoid.
Two brand-new sessions each have to redo the expensive shared analysis — the cost that forking exists to pay only once.
Resuming continues the same conversation, so the second evaluation still inherits the first's reasoning. It is sequential evaluation with an extra step.

questions.stem: Six months ago the team replaced two frequently co-called tools with a composite `get_patient_with_transfers`, and it has worked well since. A new requirement needs patient records without any transfer history; another needs transfers for a whole ward rather than for a single patient. Which three statements are sound? Select three.
options: The composite returns transfer history the patient-only requirement does not need, adding context cost.
Prompting the agent to bundle related calls into one turn saves the same round-trip without fixing the composition.
A composite hides the composition, so each new access pattern needs a new tool or an over-fetch.
Composite tools are always preferable to prompt-level bundling once a pairing is established.
The ward-level requirement is well served by calling the composite once for each patient on the ward.
Restoring the two original tools alongside the composite would reduce the agent's decision space.

whyRight.text: The corpus prefers prompting the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn over creating composite tools, because a composite hides the composition. That cost is invisible while the access pattern is stable and surfaces the moment a new pattern needs one half of the pair, or the pair at a different granularity.

whyWrong.text: This inverts the stated preference. Bundling is preferred precisely because the agent can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously without the composition being frozen into a tool.
One call per patient turns a single ward-level need into many calls, each over-fetching. It is the round-trip cost the composite was built to remove, reintroduced at a larger scale.
Adding tools enlarges the decision space rather than reducing it, and three overlapping tools over the same data is the near-miss-description situation that degrades selection.

questions.stem: Adding audit hooks across the platform's 140 service files requires a discovery pass that enumerates every call site. On the last attempt the discovery output alone filled the context window before any implementation began, and the session had to be abandoned partway. What structure avoids this?
options: Run `/compact` once discovery completes, then implement inside the compacted session.
Run discovery in an Explore subagent that returns a summary; implement in the main session.
Split the work across several sessions joined with `--continue`, one per service directory.
Move the discovery pass to a larger-context model and keep both phases in one session.

whyRight.text: Context isolation used deliberately: an Explore subagent absorbs the verbose discovery output and returns a concise summary, leaving the main session's context intact for design and implementation.

whyWrong.text: `/compact` mid-task loses the precision the implementation phase needs. Compression is lossy exactly where the call-site detail matters.
Multiple sessions stitched together add coordination overhead and consistency risk, and each session still has to carry its own discovery output.
A bigger window postpones the problem and raises cost without changing the structure: verbose discovery still occupies the same context the implementation needs.

questions.stem: Conventions differ by area: scheduling services use a repository pattern, the interoperability adapters use async pipelines, and test files follow a fixture naming scheme. Files from all three areas sit side by side in most directories rather than in separate trees. Where do these conventions belong?
options: In the root `CLAUDE.md`, organised under a heading for each of the three areas.
In a separate `CLAUDE.md` inside each subdirectory that contains the relevant files.
In `.claude/rules/` files with glob patterns matching each area's file paths.
In one skill per area, invoked explicitly whenever work on that area begins.

whyRight.text: `.claude/rules/` files carry glob frontmatter and load only when Claude works on matching files. That is deterministic file-path matching, and it is what makes conventions correct regardless of which directory the work happens in — the decisive property when file types are interleaved.

whyWrong.text: Headings in one always-loaded file rely on the model inferring which section applies to the file in front of it, rather than on deterministic path matching.
Per-directory files work poorly when the three file types are spread across the same directories — every directory would need all three conventions anyway.
Skills are for workflow-specific guidance invoked on demand. These are conventions that must apply automatically whenever a matching file is touched.

questions.stem: Your onboarding agent is configured with `allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]` and a system prompt instructing it to delegate deep dives to specialist subagents. It never delegates — it attempts everything itself, and its sessions run long and stay shallow. Which two statements are correct? Select two.
options: The configuration withholds `Task`, so the agent cannot spawn a subagent at all.
A system prompt cannot grant a capability that the tool configuration does not include.
Adding subagent descriptions to the system prompt would enable spawning once they are named.
Rewriting the delegation instruction more forcefully is the appropriate first fix here.
The agent needs `Write` access before it is permitted to create a subagent.

whyRight.text: A coordinator's `allowedTools` must include `Task` — without it the agent cannot spawn subagents regardless of what its prompt says. The prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds.

whyWrong.text: Descriptions identify what a subagent type is for; they do not enable spawning. The `Task` tool does.
Rewriting the instruction is the corpus's named wrong answer for this symptom. No wording reaches a capability that is absent from the configuration.
`Write` governs file creation and has no bearing on delegation. Spawning is gated by `Task` alone.

questions.stem: The agent holds a general `run_query` tool for the reporting database so that it can answer schema questions during exploration. It has started using that tool to run ad-hoc aggregate queries against live patient tables, which the compliance team has now flagged twice. What is the durable fix?
options: Add a system-prompt rule forbidding queries against patient tables during exploration.
Block the patient table names at the query layer and reject any statement referencing them.
Remove `run_query` and have the agent ask a human whenever it needs schema information.
Replace `run_query` with a `describe_schema` tool that returns structure and cannot return rows.

whyRight.text: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained alternative enforces the boundary at the interface level. The agent's legitimate need is schema information, and a tool that can only return structure makes the misuse impossible rather than discouraged.

whyWrong.text: Prompt instructions are probabilistic. For a boundary that must hold, the corpus is explicit that the fix belongs at the interface, not in the prompt.
A denylist of table names is fragile and not future-proof — it needs updating for every new table, and the tool remains capable of arbitrary row access.
Removing the capability entirely blocks a legitimate need and pushes a routine question onto a human. Least privilege means the minimum tools required, not fewer.

questions.stem: The provisioning repository's review job was added last week, and every run hangs until the runner's 30-minute timeout kills it. No output is ever written to the job log. The command in the workflow file reads `claude "Review this diff for regressions"`. What is missing?
options: The `-p` flag, which processes the prompt, prints to stdout and exits.
The `--batch` flag, which tells Claude Code that it is running unattended.
A `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` environment variable set on the job.
A redirect of `stdin` from `/dev/null` so the process cannot block waiting on input.

whyRight.text: `-p` (or `--print`) is the documented non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, prints to stdout and exits. Without it Claude Code waits for interactive input, which in a pipeline means hanging until the runner kills the job.

whyWrong.text: `--batch` does not exist. It is one of the corpus's named trap options for this question.
`CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is not a real environment variable, and no variable substitutes for the print flag.
Redirecting stdin is a Unix workaround that may stop the hang by starving the prompt, but it is not the documented approach and produces no usable output.

questions.stem: Six weeks of review data: style findings run at 54% false positive, documentation at 47%, security at 7%, performance at 16%. Engineers have begun dismissing every comment the job posts, security findings included, and two genuine vulnerabilities were closed unread last sprint. What should the team do?
options: Display a confidence score beside each finding so that engineers can triage them themselves.
Reduce strictness uniformly across all four categories until the overall false-positive rate falls.
Temporarily disable the style and documentation categories while their prompts are improved.
Add few-shot examples across all four categories and let the rate improve over the coming weeks.

whyRight.text: High-false-positive categories cause engineers to dismiss everything, including accurate findings in high-precision categories. Surgically disabling the noisy categories stops the trust bleed immediately while the prompts behind them are fixed.

whyWrong.text: Confidence scores still surface every finding. The volume of noise — and the dismissal habit it created — is unchanged.
Uniform reduction damages the security and performance categories, which are already precise, in order to quieten two that are not.
This is the right repair on the wrong timescale. Trust continues eroding across the weeks it takes, and by then engineers ignore the job entirely.

questions.stem: Findings currently arrive as prose in the job log, and a script scrapes them with regular expressions to post inline pull-request comments. The scraper has broken three times this quarter whenever phrasing shifted. Each comment needs a file path, a line number, a severity and a suggested fix. What should replace the scraper?
options: An "Output Format" section added to the repository's `CLAUDE.md` specifying the four fields.
A run using `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`, so the output is machine-parseable.
A prompt-level format specification with one worked example of a correctly shaped finding.
A scraper rewritten to match on keywords rather than full patterns, tolerating phrasing drift.

whyRight.text: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` enforces the schema and guarantees well-formed output that downstream tools can parse — precisely the case where findings must be turned into structured GitHub API calls carrying path, line, severity and fix.

whyWrong.text: `CLAUDE.md` guidance is not a guarantee of consistent output shape. It influences behaviour; it does not enforce a contract a parser can rely on.
Format instructions in the prompt produce variable compliance. That variability is what the scraper is already failing on.
A more forgiving scraper is still parsing free text. It trades one class of brittleness for another rather than removing the ambiguity at the source.

questions.stem: Each time an author pushes a follow-up commit, the review job re-posts near-identical comments on code that has not changed, with slightly different wording every run. Some threads now run to dozens of comments and authors have started resolving them unread. What should the re-run prompt include?
options: An instruction to comment only on lines present in the latest commit's diff.
A raised severity threshold, so that fewer findings are posted on any given run.
An instruction to start from a blank slate each run so the review stays objective.
The previous run's findings, with an instruction to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.

whyRight.text: Feeding the prior run's findings into the re-run prompt keeps the reviewer consistent across runs and stops it re-litigating settled findings. The instruction to report only new or unresolved issues is what prevents duplicate inline comments on unchanged code.

whyWrong.text: Restricting to the latest diff suppresses duplicates by also suppressing legitimate findings on code the new commit interacts with but does not touch.
A higher threshold reduces the number of comments without addressing why the same comment reappears. The duplicates that clear the bar still duplicate.
Blank-slate re-runs are the cause, not the cure. Objectivity is not improved by discarding what the reviewer already concluded — it produces exactly this flood.

questions.stem: A pull request touching eighteen files receives a detailed review on four of them, cursory notes on the rest, and one pattern flagged in one file yet explicitly approved in another. Re-running the job produces a different four files. Which two changes address the cause? Select two.
options: Run a per-file pass that reviews each file individually for issues local to it.
Run a separate integration pass examining cross-file relationships and data flows.
Move the job to a model with a larger context window so all eighteen files fit comfortably.
Instruct the reviewer to spend equal effort on every file present in the diff.
Reject pull requests above ten files so that reviews stay within a reliable size.

whyRight.text: The symptoms — depth on some files, shallowness on others, contradictory verdicts on the same pattern — are attention dilution from processing many items at once. The fix is focused passes: one per-file pass for local issues, then a separate integration pass for cross-file concerns.

whyWrong.text: A larger context window does not fix attention quality. The corpus names this as the trap: the dilution exists regardless of window size.
Instructing the model to distribute effort evenly does not change how attention behaves across a large single pass. It restates the desired outcome.
Capping pull-request size is a process constraint imposed to work around a solvable architectural problem, and large changes will still legitimately occur.

questions.stem: A weekly dependency-audit job runs on the Message Batches API, and its report must reach the platform lead 30 hours after submission. The schedule is being fixed now. The team is planning around batches that have so far always completed within about an hour. What submission window does the SLA actually permit?
options: Six hours — the batch must be submitted at least 24 hours before the deadline.
Twenty-nine hours, leaving an hour of headroom over the typical completion time.
Thirty hours, since batch results are returned as soon as processing finishes.
Twenty-four hours, because the processing window and the deadline are the same figure.

whyRight.text: The Batch API has a processing window of up to 24 hours and no latency SLA, so planning must absorb the worst case: submission deadline equals downstream deadline minus 24 hours. With 30 hours available, the usable submission window is six hours.

whyWrong.text: This plans around the typical case. There is no SLA, so the single batch that takes 23 hours blows the deadline — the exact failure the worst-case rule prevents.
Results do return when processing finishes, but you cannot schedule against a completion time that carries no guarantee. The budget must assume the full window.
Confusing the two figures. Twenty-four hours is what must be subtracted from the deadline, not the window that remains after subtracting it.

questions.stem: The pipeline's remediation step can apply mechanical fixes automatically. Twice now it has rewritten more than 200 files in a single run after a shared formatting rule changed, and both runs reached the default branch. Policy states that any change touching over 50 files requires human approval. Where does that rule belong?
options: In the review prompt, as an instruction to stop and ask before any large-scale rewrite.
In a `PostToolUse` hook that reverts the change once the file count is exceeded.
In a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks the operation above the threshold and routes it for approval.
In the tool's own description, stating that it must not be used on more than 50 files.

whyRight.text: `PreToolUse` fires before the tool executes and can validate or block. Threshold enforcement — blocking operations above a defined size and routing them to escalation — is its primary use case, and it is deterministic: it fires regardless of how the model behaves.

whyWrong.text: Prompt instructions are probabilistic. For safety-critical enforcement the corpus is explicit that hooks, not prompts, carry the rule.
`PostToolUse` fires after the tool has run, so the 200 files are already rewritten. Reverting is messier and less certain than never executing.
A description shapes tool selection, not tool authorisation. Nothing enforces a limit expressed only as guidance in the description text.

questions.stem: Generated tests for the circuit-activation service compile and pass, but they ignore the team's fixture conventions, assert on internals rather than on behaviour, and duplicate scenarios the existing suite already covers. Roughly half of each generated batch is discarded in review. What supplies the missing context to the CI-invoked run?
options: A longer prompt describing the conventions in prose at the point of invocation.
`CLAUDE.md` for the standards, plus the existing test files in context to avoid duplicates.
A post-generation filter that discards any test whose assertions overlap an existing one.
A `.claude/rules/` file scoped by glob to the generated-test output directory.

whyRight.text: `CLAUDE.md` is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude project context — testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria. Supplying the existing test files in context is separately named as what stops generation from proposing scenarios the suite already covers.

whyWrong.text: Restating conventions in every invocation duplicates what project configuration exists to hold, and still gives the run no visibility of the existing suite.
Filtering afterwards discards work already paid for and misses semantically equivalent duplicates that do not overlap textually.
Path-scoped rules load when Claude works on matching files. They address conventions, not the duplicate-scenario half of the problem, which needs the existing tests in context.

questions.stem: Review comments vary in shape from run to run: sometimes a bare observation, sometimes a fix, sometimes a paragraph of surrounding context. The prompt already specifies the required format across three sentences, and tightening that wording twice has changed nothing. What is the effective next move?
options: Restate the format requirements more explicitly, enumerating each required element in turn.
Lower the temperature so that output varies less between runs.
Add ten examples covering the full range of finding types the job encounters.
Add three or four examples showing the exact required shape: issue, location, concrete fix.

whyRight.text: When instructions are already failing, refining them further is not the lever. Three to four few-shot examples showing the exact required format — identified issue, location in code, concrete fix — is the corpus's answer for inconsistent review output despite explicit instructions.

whyWrong.text: The instructions are already explicit and already failing. More explicit prose is the approach that has not worked.
Temperature controls randomness, not adherence to a specific output shape. It is the corpus's named wrong answer for suppressing an unwanted response pattern.
Ten examples of clear cases add token overhead without targeting the problem. Examples should be few and aimed at where output actually goes wrong.

questions.stem: A review of the activation module raised three issues: a race in the retry path, a lock-ordering defect that the retry path depends on, and a misspelled log string. You are feeding these back for fixes and want to avoid a second round of rework. Which three statements are sound? Select three.
options: The race and the lock-ordering defect belong in one message, because their fixes interact.
Fixing the retry race without the new locking design in view can produce a conflicting patch.
The log-string typo is independent and can be sent separately or alongside without risk.
Every issue should be sent one at a time so that each iteration stays focused and verifiable.
All three belong in one message purely because they were found in the same review pass.
Interdependent issues should be ordered by severity and then fixed strictly in that sequence.

whyRight.text: Interacting issues go in one detailed message so Claude can design a single coherent change; independent ones can iterate separately. Fixing the retry path without knowing the new locking design is the specific way separate fixes to interacting problems collide.

whyWrong.text: Strict one-at-a-time is wrong for interdependent issues — the sequential locking fix and retry fix can contradict each other and force another round.
Shared provenance is not the criterion. Whether fixes interact is what decides batching, and the typo interacts with nothing.
Severity ordering still fixes interacting defects one at a time, which is the pattern that produces conflicting patches. They need designing together, not sequencing.

questions.stem: The prompt instructs the reviewer to "check that comments are accurate." It now flags every comment that is merely terse or slightly out of date — around sixty per pull request — burying the handful that actively describe the wrong behaviour. How should the criterion be rewritten?
options: Flag a comment only where the behaviour it claims contradicts what the code actually does.
Flag comments that have not been updated since the code beneath them last changed.
Rate each comment's accuracy on a four-point scale and report only the lowest band.
Check comment accuracy only in files the pull request modifies, ignoring the rest.

whyRight.text: When vague instructions produce inconsistent output, move from abstract to concrete. The corpus uses this exact pair: "check that comments are accurate" replaced by "flag comments only when the behaviour they claim contradicts the code's actual behaviour" — an explicit, testable criterion.

whyWrong.text: Staleness is a proxy, not the property that matters. A comment untouched for two years can be perfectly accurate; one edited yesterday can be wrong.
A rating scale without defined criteria simply relocates the vagueness into the scale. The model still has no testable definition of what accurate means.
Narrowing the scope reduces the volume of noise without improving precision. The same wrong comments are flagged, just fewer of them.

questions.stem: The pipeline generates a migration script and then, in the same session, asks for a review of that script. Reviews come back clean; defects surface later in staging, three times this quarter. A colleague suggests adding "be more critical" to the review step's prompt. What is the actual problem?
options: The review step runs before the migration script has been written to disk.
Review criteria are absent, so the step has nothing concrete to evaluate against.
The session that generated the script retains its reasoning and reviews its own work poorly.
Migration scripts need schema context that the pipeline supplies to neither step.

whyRight.text: The same session that generated code is less effective at reviewing its own changes: it retains its reasoning context and is less likely to challenge its own decisions. The fix is an independent instance, and no instruction to be more critical substitutes for that.

whyWrong.text: Nothing in the stem indicates a sequencing fault, and a review of a non-existent file would fail loudly rather than return clean.
Explicit criteria genuinely improve review quality, but they do not remove the anchoring. The same session applies them to reasoning it already endorsed.
Missing schema context would degrade generation as well as review. The signal here is specifically that self-review passes and independent staging does not.

questions.stem: The triage step must always return a structured verdict, but roughly one run in twelve comes back as a paragraph of prose instead of a tool call, and the downstream parser fails on it. Three verdict tools are defined, one per severity band. Which two statements are correct? Select two.
options: Setting `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` guarantees a tool call rather than conversational text.
With three tools defined, `{"type": "any"}` still lets the model pick the best-fitting one.
`{"type": "auto"}` plus a firm prompt instruction gives the same guarantee more flexibly.
`{"type": "tool", "name": ...}` is required whenever more than one tool could apply.
Prose responses indicate the tool schemas are invalid and are being silently rejected.

whyRight.text: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees the model calls some tool and never returns conversational text; where several extraction or verdict tools exist, it still selects the best-fitting one. That combination is exactly what this situation needs.

whyWrong.text: `auto` permits a text response by design, and the prompt instruction is probabilistic. That pairing is the current configuration and the current failure.
Forcing one named tool is for guaranteeing a specific first step. Here any of the three may be correct depending on severity, so pinning one would be wrong.
An invalid schema produces an error, not a fluent paragraph. Prose output is the documented behaviour of `auto` when the model judges text sufficient.

questions.stem: Engineers dismiss roughly a third of all findings, but the team cannot tell which kinds are noise and which are being waved through unfairly. Dismissals are currently recorded as a timestamp and a username, with no reference to what was flagged. What change makes the pattern analysable?
options: Require a free-text reason on every dismissal so the team can read back through them.
Add a `detected_pattern` field to each finding and group dismissal rates by that field.
Record which reviewer dismissed each finding so individual thresholds can be compared.
Sample ten dismissed findings a week and review them manually for recurring themes.

whyRight.text: A `detected_pattern` field identifies which construct triggered each finding, so dismissals can be grouped by pattern to reveal which ones drive false positives. That turns an undifferentiated dismissal rate into a diagnosis.

whyWrong.text: Free-text reasons are unstructured and do not aggregate. The team ends up with a third as many prose notes as findings and no way to rank causes.
Reviewer identity explains who dismissed, not what kind of finding is noisy. The same noisy pattern would show up across every reviewer.
Manual sampling is slow, small and subject to the same categorisation problem — the themes still have to be invented by hand rather than emerging from a field.

questions.stem: A number-porting script mishandles rows where the donor-carrier field is null. Three rounds of describing the defect in prose have produced three partial fixes, each of which broke something that previously worked. The failure reproduces reliably on a local sample. Which two moves converge fastest? Select two.
options: Supply a concrete failing case: a sample row containing nulls and the exact expected output.
Iterate by feeding back the specific test failures until the suite runs green.
Describe the null-handling requirement more emphatically, covering every field that can be null.
Ask for a rewrite of the whole script, given that three attempts have now failed.
Write the tests after the fix lands, to verify that the behaviour is finally correct.

whyRight.text: Providing a specific failing test case with example input and expected output is named as the fastest way to fix an edge case such as nulls in a migration script, and test-driven iteration then feeds concrete failures back until everything is green.

whyWrong.text: Prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently — three rounds of exactly this have already failed. Emphasis is not the missing ingredient.
A full rewrite discards working behaviour and re-runs the same underspecified brief. Nothing has been added that would make attempt four differ from attempt three.
Tests written after the fact are verification, not test-driven iteration. Writing them first is what anchors each iteration to a concrete failure signal.

questions.stem: The schema marks `fumigation_certificate_number` as required and non-nullable, because settlement needs it. Roughly one consignment in six ships without fumigation, and those documents genuinely carry no such number. Those records now hold plausible-looking numbers that match nothing in the fumigation registry. What is the correct schema change?
options: Add a validation rule that rejects any certificate number failing a checksum test.
Retry extraction on those records with a prompt emphasising accuracy over completeness.
Keep the field required and route every affected record to a human for confirmation.
Make the field nullable so the model can return `null` when the document has no number.

whyRight.text: A required, non-nullable field pushes the model to fabricate values to satisfy the schema when the information is absent. Marking fields required only when the information is always available — and nullable otherwise — lets the model return `null` instead of hallucinating.

whyWrong.text: A checksum catches some fabrications and misses any invention that happens to be well-formed. It also leaves the pressure to fabricate fully in place.
No feedback can conjure data the document does not contain. Retrying burns tokens and, under a required field, increases the pressure toward fabrication.
This spends review capacity confirming an absence the schema could express directly, and does nothing about the fabricated values already being produced.

questions.stem: Overall extraction accuracy sits at 97%, and the team proposes auto-processing everything above the confidence threshold from next month. Phytosanitary declarations account for about 4% of volume, arrive in three languages, and nobody has measured their accuracy separately. What should happen before the change?
options: Raise the confidence threshold until the aggregate accuracy figure reaches 99%.
Measure accuracy by document type and by field, confirming that every segment clears the bar.
Auto-process the high-confidence stream and watch the aggregate figure for any decline.
Route all phytosanitary declarations to human review and auto-process the remaining volume.

whyRight.text: An aggregate 97% can hide a 40% failure rate on one rare document type — overall metrics average away segment-level failures. Before reducing human review, validate accuracy by document type and by field, and require every segment to meet the bar independently.

whyWrong.text: Moving the threshold changes how much is auto-processed without revealing how the rare segments behave. A masked 40% failure stays masked at any aggregate figure.
A 4% segment failing badly barely moves a 97% aggregate, so the monitor would not fire. This is the masking problem used as the detection mechanism.
This guesses which segment is weak instead of measuring. It may divert capacity to a segment that performs well while a different one fails unseen.

questions.stem: Weighbridge tickets list individual bag weights and a stated net total. Reconciliation discovers, weeks after release and after settlement has already run, that the two sometimes disagree by several tonnes. What should the extraction produce so that the disagreement surfaces at extraction time instead?
options: Both the stated total and a total re-derived from the line items, with a conflict flag.
A monthly reconciliation report comparing stated totals against summed line items.
A prompt instruction to double-check the arithmetic before returning the extracted record.
A confidence score on the total field, with low-confidence totals routed to review.

whyRight.text: The self-correction pattern is structural: extract the claimed value and an independently derived value, then flag disagreement with a boolean. `stated_total`, `calculated_total` and `conflict_detected` catch arithmetic drift on every record and produce a machine-readable signal at extraction time.

whyWrong.text: A monthly report is the current situation with a shorter delay. Detection still happens after release rather than before it.
"Be careful with totals" is a vague instruction with no detection mechanism. Nothing downstream can tell whether the check happened.
Confidence expresses how sure the model is about what it read, not whether the numbers are internally consistent. A confidently misread total scores high.

questions.stem: High-confidence extractions are now processed without human review, and they account for roughly 80% of volume. The team wants to keep measuring the true error rate of that automated path without re-reviewing everything it emits. Which two properties should the audit sample have? Select two.
options: It is drawn at random from the high-confidence stream, not only from flagged items.
It is stratified across document types and field categories rather than volume-weighted.
It is drawn from the lowest-confidence extractions, where errors are most likely to appear.
It is drawn from the most common document type, which represents most of the throughput.
It is replaced by a full re-review of every document once each quarter.

whyRight.text: Even high-confidence extractions need regular auditing of a random sample, stratified across document types and field categories rather than taken off the top of the review queue. That is what measures the true error rate of the automated path and detects novel error patterns before they compound.

whyWrong.text: Reviewing only the lowest-confidence items leaves novel error patterns in the automated stream undetected — which is the stream the team just stopped reviewing.
Sampling the most common type under-samples the rare, worst-performing segments, which are precisely the ones an aggregate figure already hides.
A quarterly full re-review defeats the automation and does not scale. Calibration exists to make oversight targeted, not periodic and total.

questions.stem: Validation fails on `container_seal_number` for 60 consignments, and the loop retries each of them three times before giving up. Investigation shows all 60 moved as break-bulk cargo, which uses no containers and therefore carries no seals at all. What is the right response?
options: Raise the retry limit to ten so the model has more opportunities to locate the field.
Strengthen the retry feedback message to state precisely which field is missing.
Make the field nullable, accept the absence as a valid answer, and stop retrying.
Keep the field required and flag all 60 for manual entry by the operations team.

whyRight.text: Retry-with-feedback fixes only errors the model can correct from the provided context — format, structure, arithmetic. When information is genuinely absent from the source, retries burn tokens for nothing and the pressure to fill a required field invites fabrication. The fix is schema design.

whyWrong.text: Absent information stays absent. Ten attempts extract exactly as much as three from a document that never carried a seal number.
No feedback can conjure missing data. The model already knows which field failed; what it lacks is a value that exists.
Manual entry asks a human to supply a number that does not exist either. It converts a schema-design problem into recurring operational cost.

questions.stem: An inspection certificate records moisture content at 12.4%. The fumigation record for the same lot, issued the same day by a different inspector, records 13.1%. Both documents are authentic, neither is obviously superseded, and settlement tolerances turn on this figure. What should the pipeline emit?
options: The mean of the two readings, with a note recording that the sources disagreed.
The inspection certificate's figure, since moisture content is that document's primary purpose.
A validation failure that holds the lot until a human resolves the discrepancy.
Both values with their sources, explicitly annotated as a conflict for downstream reconciliation.

whyRight.text: When sources conflict, complete the analysis carrying both values, annotate the conflict with source attribution, and let the coordinator or a human reconcile. Resolving autonomously abandons a decision that sits above the pipeline's scope.

whyWrong.text: Averaging invents a third figure that appears on neither document, and quietly destroys the evidence that a discrepancy existed.
Applying a heuristic to pick the more likely value is exactly the autonomous resolution the pattern forbids. Both documents are authentic.
Blocking the pipeline before analysis completes is unnecessary. The correct behaviour is to finish, annotate, and pass the conflict onward.

questions.stem: The pipeline validates every extracted record in code after the model returns it, on top of the `tool_use` schema that already constrains the shape. An engineer proposes deleting that validation layer as duplicated effort, noting that the schema already enforces types, required fields and enum membership. Which response is correct?
options: Keep it: no JSON schema can express that a stated net weight equals the sum of its bag weights.
Delete it — the schema enforces the contract at generation time, so the second pass only adds latency.
Keep it, but only for fields the schema marks optional, where the model has the most latitude.
Replace both layers with a stricter schema encoding the cross-field rules as nested constraints.

whyRight.text: Tool use enforces structure at generation time, but code should still validate semantic and business rules no JSON schema can express — a cross-field sum, a date ordering — plus defence in depth for whatever consumes the record downstream. The schema constrains shape; the validator checks meaning.

whyWrong.text: This is the named misconception. Structural enforcement at generation time says nothing about whether the values are right, and removing the layer removes the only check on business rules.
Optionality is unrelated to semantic risk. A required, well-typed tonnage field can still be wrong, and cross-field rules span required fields by definition.
